So ACID became a core part of them, and the transaction became the core component of a relational database.

answer: Indexes make reads faster and writes slower: every index is one more structure each write has to update.
evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'indexes make reads faster and writes slower. Every index is one more structure each write has to update.'

answer: Core idea: acquire the lock before you proceed (Database Locking: Pessimistic Locking). Flow: ACQ_LOCK(), then READ and UPDATE (the critical section), then REL_LOCK(); every transaction waits to acquire the lock, and only after the release may another transaction do the same.
evidence: Ch1 §1.2: 'its core idea is that you acquire the lock before you proceed'; Fig 1·a: 'ACQ_LOCK(), then READ and UPDATE, then REL_LOCK().'

answer: count++ is not atomic (read, add, write). Two people clap on the same Medium story at the same moment: both transactions read the same old count and both write back count + 1, so the final value is count + 1, not count + 2: a lost update. Locking protects the sanity (consistency and integrity) of data against concurrent updates. (Note: a single UPDATE ... SET count = count + 1 is itself safe; lost updates come from reading into the app and writing back.)
evidence: Ch1 §1.2: 'Take two people clapping on a Medium story at the same moment... Both transactions read the same old count and both write it back plus one, so the final value is count + 1, not the count + 2'; 'To protect the sanity of the data, its consistency and integrity, against concurrent updates.'

answer: Take a lock where the correctness of the data matters more than throughput (lock before you update); where correctness isn't important, it is fine to skip the lock.
evidence: Ch1 §1.2 rule: 'Take a lock where the correctness of the data matters more than throughput. Where it doesn't, skip it.'

answer: T1 holds row 2 and wants (waits for) a lock on row 1, which T2 holds; T2 holds row 1 and wants row 2, which T1 holds. The waits form a cycle so nobody moves forward, like the OS deadlock. The board labelled it 'Risk: Transactional Deadlock!!' and noted the transaction that detects it is killed.
evidence: Ch1 §1.5 and Fig 1·e: 'T1 holds row 2 and wants a lock on row 1, which T2 holds. T2 wants a lock on row 2, which T1 holds. Nobody moves forward.'

answer: Check whether it can deadlock: arrange your statements and the order in which you acquire and release locks, and if a deadlock is possible, protect against it (in any language). The standard defence is to lock rows in one fixed order, e.g. ascending primary key.
evidence: Ch1 §1.5: 'whenever you write code or a SQL query that takes locks, in any language, check whether it can deadlock. Arrange your statements, and the order in which you acquire and release locks... protect against it. The standard defence is a single order'.

answer: They don't let a deadlock persist: whenever a lock would make a transaction wait, the database runs a deadlock-detection algorithm (a cycle in the waits-for graph). If granting the lock would create a deadlock, the engine kills the transaction that fired that query, so the cycle-closing edge never forms ('the transaction that detects the deadlock kills itself'). Caveats: InnoDB checks at once and tries to pick the smaller transaction as victim (ERROR 1213, whole txn rolled back); PostgreSQL waits deadlock_timeout (1 s) first and its victim choice is unpredictable; Oracle rolls back one statement of the detecting transaction. Every transaction must be ready to retry.
evidence: Ch1 §1.5: 'Whenever a lock would make a transaction wait, the database runs a deadlock detection algorithm'; 'the database engine kills the transaction that fired that query'; More precisely note on InnoDB/PostgreSQL/Oracle.

answer: If it entered a deadlock everything would stall and nothing would move forward; the only way out would be to reboot the database, which means downtime. (Short of reboot, a lock-wait timeout, 50 s default, or killing a session also breaks it.)
evidence: Ch1 §1.5: 'If a database did enter a deadlock, everything would stall... The only way out would be to reboot the database, which means downtime, so databases never let it happen.'

answer: Start two transactions on two rows (e.g. two terminals connected to a local MySQL, SET autocommit = 0, begin a transaction in each) and take locks crosswise: T1 locks row 2, T2 locks row 1, then T1 asks for row 1 and T2 asks for row 2. When that final lock-acquiring query fires, the transaction that fired it is killed.
evidence: Ch1 §1.5 'See it yourself' and §1.7 'Try it in two terminals'.

answer: Shared locks = read locks, taken with SELECT ... FOR SHARE (older MySQL spelling LOCK IN SHARE MODE). Exclusive locks = write locks, taken with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'Shared locks are also called read locks; exclusive locks are also called write locks... end it with FOR SHARE'; 'To take an exclusive lock, end the SELECT with FOR UPDATE.'

answer: From the page: (1) the holder can read the row; (2) other transactions can read (and share-lock) it too; (3) no other transaction may modify it - the rows are reserved for read by the current transaction; (4) T1 (holder) may read and modify, T2 may only read, and must wait to update until T1 commits or aborts. (Caveat: while both hold shared locks, neither can update; if both try, deadlock.)
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'A shared lock lets the holder read the row and lets other transactions read it too, but no other transaction may modify it. The board called the rows reserved for read by the current transaction'; 'T1 may read and modify the row; T2 may only read and wait.'

answer: T1 gets shared locks on rows 1, 2, 6; T2 also gets its shared locks on 3, 4, 6 even though row 6 is already share-locked, so both may read row 6. If T2 tries to update row 6 it waits until T1 commits or aborts. More precisely, T1 can't update row 6 either while T2 shares it; if both try to update, each waits on the other and the DB detects a deadlock and rolls one back.
evidence: Ch1 §1.3 and Fig 1·b, plus the More precisely note.

answer: Very high read throughput for read-only use cases: other transactions can still read the locked rows, while modification is prevented.
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'Shared locks give very high read throughput for read-only use cases'.

answer: Its read lock is raised to an exclusive lock implicitly (without you doing anything), and only then does the modification happen. This upgrade is a classic deadlock source: if two transactions both hold the shared lock and both try to update, each waits for the other and InnoDB rolls one back.
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'its read lock is raised to an exclusive lock implicitly... The upgrade is a classic source of deadlock'.

answer: Really strict: other transactions are not even allowed to read the locked rows, let alone modify them; the rows are reserved for write by the current transaction. Any update requires an exclusive lock. (Caveat: under MVCC plain SELECTs still read the last committed version; it blocks modifications and other locking reads, except InnoDB SERIALIZABLE with autocommit off.)
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'other transactions are not even allowed to read the locked rows, let alone modify them: the rows are reserved for write by the current transaction'; More precisely note.

answer: T2's query does not complete; it waits until T1 commits or aborts, because of row 6 alone. If T2 had asked only for rows 3 and 4, its statement would have completed with those rows.
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'T2's query does not complete. It waits until T1 commits or aborts... Without row 6 in its set, T2's statement would have completed with rows 3 and 4.'

answer: Exclusive locks severely hurt throughput, but where you need exclusivity you have to use them.
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'Exclusive locks severely hurt throughput. But where you need exclusivity, you have to use them.'

answer: SKIP LOCKED (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) skips rows locked by another transaction - removes them from the result set - and goes ahead best-effort with the unlocked rows instead of waiting. T2 moves on at once with rows 3 and 4 (row 6 left out).
evidence: Ch1 §1.4: 'it removes the locked rows from the result set'; 'T2's query for rows 3, 4 and 6 with SKIP LOCKED moves on at once and gets rows 3 and 4 only.'

answer: When you need all the rows (then you must wait, no other option) - e.g. when a user picks a specific seat (BookMyShow 14C) you can't hand them another. It gives an inconsistent view of the data, so it is not for general transactional work; only for queue-like tables where any free row will do.
evidence: Ch1 §1.4: 'When you need all the rows, you have to wait; there is no other option'; 'an inconsistent view of the data, so it is not for general transactional work'; §2.6.

answer: A NOWAIT locking read does not wait for the lock: if any wanted row is locked by another transaction it fails immediately ('kills itself'). Board error: ERROR 3572: Do not wait for lock (MySQL; only the statement errors there, while in PostgreSQL the whole transaction becomes aborted). After failure it may retry or not, depending on business.
evidence: Ch1 §1.4: 'SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT; -- ERROR 3572: Do not wait for lock'.

answer: So you don't wait for nothing: without it T2 waits for the lock up to the query timeout (10 s in the class example), tying up that thread's share of the database and making the client wait, in a use case that doesn't care if the row is locked. (Real defaults: InnoDB innodb_lock_wait_timeout 50 s; PostgreSQL lock_timeout 0 = forever.) Teacher's image: the transaction has an existential crisis - someone else will process the row - so it kills itself.
evidence: Ch1 §1.4: 'Why have NOWAIT at all? So you don't wait for nothing...'

answer: Some goroutine found the first free row, wrote and committed before a later goroutine started its read; that later reader saw user_id no longer NULL, so WHERE user_id IS NULL handed it the next row - the condition moved it on, not the code or the transaction. (Under REPEATABLE READ the snapshot is taken at the first read.)
Only two words added at the end of the SELECT: FOR UPDATE (an exclusive lock on the row returned); the code is otherwise line for line the same.
Waiting is not deadlock. A deadlock happens when you wait on a row locked by someone who is in turn waiting on a row you hold - it needs a cycle; here transactions merely wait.

ACID holds at the level of a transaction; the check-in has concurrent transactions, and how concurrent transactions are scheduled depends on the isolation level (read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable). Defaults aren't serializable, so read-then-book can race unless you lock (FOR UPDATE) or use a conditional UPDATE.

Yes - with serializable the transactions would (as taught) run one after another and you wouldn't face the seat problem, but it's pathetically slow. It isn't used because you need high throughput and parallel writes (why should a user updating row 100 wait for one on row 1); MySQL defaults to REPEATABLE READ, PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED. More precisely serializable doesn't literally queue; you must retry on serialization failures (PG) or deadlocks (InnoDB).

The engine must treat a range query and a pointed lookup (id = 67) uniformly; a lock on one pointed row would never move to a 'next row', so 'move to the next row' can't be the rule. Instead the engine re-evaluates the statement it is running and locks what now matches (for id=67, nothing).
All 120 seats filled on every run (1.25 s, 1.73 s, 1.79 s), in order: 1C, 1D, 1E, 1F, 2A, 2B ... Correct.

First transaction gets the lock on the first free row; the others get no row yet - the DB returns a row only once the transaction holds its lock - and wait. When the holder commits/aborts, the engine signals the waiters to re-evaluate the query inside the engine; the row no longer matches user_id IS NULL, so one of the 119 locks the second row and the rest wait again; repeat for third, fourth seat... (PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED behaviour; at REPEATABLE READ waiter errors and retries.)
No. Whichever transaction gets scheduled first gets the next seat; in the run, seat 1A went to a different user than user 1.
Slow: in the worst case every waiter re-evaluates after every commit: N(N+1)/2 evaluations inside the DB, 7,260 for 120 - painful for the database (runs ~1.2-1.8 s).

Add SKIP LOCKED to the approach 4 query (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED). It completed in 147 ms vs about 1.7 s - about ten times faster - and still filled all 120 seats; ~120 evaluations instead of up to 7,260.

It still takes an exclusive lock, but seeing the row locked it moves straight on to the next row matching the WHERE and locks that for the second transaction (next for the third, etc.); nobody waits. At end of class: it doesn't re-evaluate the query at all - it reads a disk page / B+ tree node of many rows and if the first is locked moves to the next at once.
evidence: Ch2 §2.5 and 'What the engine actually reads'.

Engines differ: InnoDB keeps its lock table in memory, PostgreSQL marks row locks in the row itself (so FOR UPDATE can cause disk writes).

How users are allowed to access the value (not what it holds). Here only keys are queried, the value is a black box, so a BLOB (or varchar/long text).

A created_at column plus a ttl_sec column, with a background job that deletes keys where now() - created_at >= ttl_sec.
now() - created_at is a dynamic computation per row, so no index can be used; the DB scans every row every time the job runs.

Store the absolute expiration time expired_at (computed once at write) instead of created_at + TTL, index it, and clean up with DELETE FROM store WHERE expired_at <= now() - a range scan on the index reading only expired rows.

The single cleanup query (DELETE WHERE expired_at <= now()) matches both expired and user-deleted rows, so one job instead of two, no is_deleted column, minimal load thanks to the expired_at index - saves CPU, disk, reads and storage.

answer: Engineers habitually add one, but you don't always need it - add it only if needed; the habit comes from ORMs (makes the ORM's life simple).

By a periodic batch cron job DELETE FROM store WHERE expired_at <= now(), removing expired and soft-deleted rows together - because pointed deletes are expensive (B+ tree rebalancing per delete); batching minimizes rebalancing. (InnoDB itself delete-marks and purges later.)

Use chapter 1's locks or isolation levels - leverage what SQL gives. E.g. BEGIN; SELECT key ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT (fail at once if another put holds it); UPDATE; COMMIT. NOWAIT picked hypothetically; no right choice between SKIP LOCKED, NOWAIT, waiting - depends on desired guarantees.

Batch deletion with a cron job: every t minutes (10 in example) a hard delete DELETE FROM store WHERE expired_at < now() runs; between runs expired rows remain on disk, so reads through kv store to MySQL filter with SELECT * ... WHERE key = k AND expired_at > now().
Between runs expired keys still exist, so GET adds AND expired_at > now(): the expired value is never returned; it saves network IO on both machines and the disk read of the value.
When a key that is read is found expired, delete it on the spot (and report it doesn't exist); never searches for expired keys. Suitable for in-memory databases (Redis), not disk-based ones.

In memory a delete is just free + removing from hash table (microseconds, no rebalance, no network IO). On disk every per-key delete may require B+ tree rebalancing - pathetically slow, so batch. (InnoDB delete-marks and purges, merges pages below 50%.)
Keys that expire and are never read again would never be deleted, so a periodic job is still needed.

With millions of expired keys each run would take a long time; lazy deletion already solves ~90%; Redis is single-threaded (main thread) so cleanup time is time not serving; it optimizes speed over completeness.

Sample 20 random keys from those with an expiry; delete the expired ones in the sample; if more than 25% of the 20 were expired/deleted, repeat; once below 25%, stop. (Since Redis 6.0: incremental cursor, batches of 20, continue while >~10% stale, within CPU budget.)
A random sample of 20 is representative of the population (keys with expiry): if under 25% of the sample is expired, the population has under 25% expired-but-not-deleted keys.
3/20 = 15% < 25%: Redis deletes those 3 and stops; about 15% of the population remains expired-not-deleted, which is okay - later reads or rounds handle them.

Speed over completeness: accepts some leaked memory (expired keys up to ~25% of TTL keys, statistically ~20-25% worst case; current Redis aims ~10%) to spend minimal time in cleanup, because it's single-threaded and must leave time for get/put/delete.

Per the instructor, the central limit theorem, with a proof in a paper linked from Redis's site (no public source found; in Redis's code 20 is a tunable constant). Works up to about 5 million keys by his figure.

Add AND expired_at > now() to the user's delete UPDATE: if already expired, no write happens - saves two disk IOs (the row and the expired_at index); the batch job removes it anyway ('heads you win, tails you win'). Found in Apache Ignite's code.

Delete: UPDATE store SET expired_at = -1 WHERE key = 'k1' AND expired_at > now(); Batch cleanup: DELETE FROM store WHERE expired_at <= now(); Get: SELECT * FROM store WHERE key = 'k1' AND expired_at > now();

Not every key has a TTL; a key without one never expires, so an explicit delete must do something in the DB - the -1 marks it so the cleanup job removes it. Any magic value works (e.g. date before 1970), column type permitting.

A transaction waited longer than the set timeout for the lock holder to commit or abort. Two usual reasons: the holder genuinely does long processing (raise the timeout), or processing finished but code forgot to commit/abort. MySQL rolls back only the waiting statement; code should roll back or retry.
